item.title: Top 10 Effective Ways to Locate All `.txt` Files in a Directory Using Python
item.description:
How to Efficiently Find All .txt Files in a Directory with Python

Locating all .txt files within a specific directory can be a common task when managing data or performing file operations. Python provides versatile methods to achieve this, whether you’re working with a few files or navigating through complex directory structures. This guide outlines several effective techniques using built-in libraries and custom functions for file searching.

Method 1: Using glob Module

The simplest way to find .txt files is through the glob module. This method allows you to match files using wildcard patterns.

item.title: Top 11 Methods to Rename Multiple Files in a Directory with Python
item.description:
I’m working on an interesting challenge: Renaming multiple files in a directory using Python. For instance, consider the file named CHEESE_CHEESE_TYPE.***. The goal is to remove the prefix CHEESE_ and end up with a filename like CHEESE_TYPE.

After attempting to utilize os.path.split without much success, I explored string manipulations but encountered some hurdles. Let’s delve into effective methods to tackle this problem head-on.

Method 1: Basic File Renaming with os.rename()

The most straightforward approach employs the os module to rename files directly based on specific prefixes.

item.title: Top 7 Methods to Get a Human-Readable Version of a File Size
item.description:
Understanding How to Convert File Sizes into Human-Readable Formats

Converting file sizes from bytes to a human-readable format is essential for software applications that deal with files, as it makes the information easily understandable for users. Below are various methods to achieve this in Python.

Method 1: Using the humanize Library

The humanize library provides an excellent function, naturalsize, that converts byte sizes into human-readable formats seamlessly.

Code Example:

import humanize

disk_sizes = [1, 100, 999, 1000, 1024, 2048, 3000, 2048000000]
for size in disk_sizes:
    output = humanize.naturalsize(size)
    print(f"{output} | {size} bytes")

Sample Output:

1 Byte | 1
100 Bytes | 100
1.0 kB | 1000
2.0 KiB | 2048
1.9 GiB | 2048000000

Method 2: A Custom Function for Human-Readable Sizes

You can create a custom function to convert bytes into a configurable human-readable format.
